title: Orsen and the Bell
premise: Elodie Villalobos, a property surveyor sent to appraise the derelict Halloway farmhouse, records strange sleep-talk audio that answers back in a second voice — the founders of the town, who bound a hungry thing beneath the bell in the orchard and left the ritual unfinished. As the harvest moon approaches, the house begins appraising Elodie in return, measuring whether they belong. With the help of the last Halloway descendant and the town's outcasts, Elodie completes the founders' interrupted rite, ringing the bell with a name freely given instead of one taken by force. The entity is released into the earth, the house goes quiet, and Elodie — who never believed — finally has a place to stay.
about_author: Casper Eriksen is the pen name of a former rural assessor who spent a decade walking empty houses across the northern plains and never quite shook the feeling that some of them were taking notes. They write horror about paperwork, property lines, and the things that live in the margins of official records.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. Sent to value the condemned Halloway farmhouse, Elodie finds rooms that measure differently on each visit and a bell tower missing its bell. That night, their recorder captures them answering questions in their sleep — questions asked in a second voice. The emotional beat is professional detachment beginning to crack; Elodie files it as equipment malfunction and stays another night anyway.

chapters.title: Second Voice
chapters.summary: POV Elodie, with interludes from the recordings themselves. The voice identifies itself as Abigail Halloway and explains the founders buried something under the orchard, caged by a bell rung with stolen names. Elodie meets Ruth, the last Halloway, who confirms the family fled mid-ritual generations ago. The beat is reluctant alliance: Elodie still doesn't believe, but starts keeping the recorder running on purpose.

chapters.title: What the House Weighs
chapters.summary: POV alternating between Elodie and Ruth. The house begins appraising them — doors opening onto rooms from their pasts, walls inscribed with their debts and shames. The entity beneath the orchard wakes early, feeding on the town's outcasts first. Ruth reveals the ritual requires a name given freely at the bell, and the founders' stolen names are why it failed. The beat is terror sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. On the night of the full moon, Elodie digs up the bell, carries it through a house trying to keep them, and rings it at the orchard's heart speaking their own name aloud — offered, not taken. The ground opens, takes what was owed, and closes. Dawn finds the house ordinary, appraised and appraising nothing. The beat is quiet belonging: Elodie, who never believed, asks Ruth if the guest room is still available.
